synthesis.coherent-face-vector-real-slic.formal:
Let $u' = (1,1,1)$, $f_{\pm} = (1, \zeta^{\pm 1}, \zeta^{\mp 1})$ with $\zeta = e^{2\pi I_4/3}$ (numbers, the components of face vectors and the module's complex structure are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, the module read on the tower's floors, where $I_4$ commutes with the tower vectors, and the bar reverses $I_4$), $C(v) = \sum_{k} v_{k}^{2}$ the bracket form and $P_{s} = \J/3$, $P_{d} = 1 - P_{s}$, as in Proposition \claimref{families.chart-computation-sign-twist-bracket-form}; write $\|v\|^{2} = \sum_{k}|v_{k}|^{2}$. By Proposition \claimref{families.rigidity-pairing-sector-one-event} the coherent face vector of every antisymmetric pairing is
\[
v \;=\; \kappa\,\bigl(u' + w f_{+}\bigr), \qquad w = \lambda e^{I_4\chi},\ \lambda \ge 0,
\]
with $\kappa \neq 0$, and $\kappa \in -I_4\R_{>0}$ when the pairing strength $\tau$ is real. Call a real structure on face space $S_{3}$-equivariant if it is an antilinear involution commuting with the face action $\Omega \mapsto \pm P\Omega$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The $S_{3}$-equivariant real structures are exactly $\sigma_{x,y} = (xP_{s} + yP_{d}) \circ \overline{\phantom{v}}$ with $|x| = |y| = 1$; $\sigma_{x,y}$ is compatible with $C$, $C(\sigma v) = \overline{C(v)}$, exactly when $x, y \in \{\pm 1\}$, and on the fixed slices of $\sigma_{1,-1}$ and $\sigma_{-1,1}$ the form $C$ restricts to $\pm(t^{2} - Q(d))$, the equal-coefficient member of Proposition \claimref{families.koide-nullity-condition-one-member-invariant}.
\item[(ii)] For $\lambda > 0$ no complex multiple of $v$ lies in the fixed slice of any $\sigma_{x,y}$, whatever the channel phase $\chi$: the doublet part of $v$ lies on the $C$-null Fourier line $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}\,f_{+}$, which contains no complex multiple of a real vector.
\item[(iii)] For every $\sigma_{x,y}$ the doublet part $d$ of the projection $\tfrac12(v + \sigma_{x,y}v)$ has $Q(d) = \tfrac12\|P_{d}v\|^{2} = \tfrac32|\kappa|^{2}\lambda^{2}$, independent of $x$, $y$ and $\chi$. For $\kappa \in -I_4\R_{>0}$ the $C$-compatible structures whose slice contains the singlet $\kappa u'$ are $\sigma_{-1,-1}$ (Euclidean) and $\sigma_{-1,1}$ (Lorentzian, $C = -(t^{2} - Q(d))$ on its slice); in the real coordinates of these slices the projected vector is
\[
p_{k} \;=\; |\kappa|\bigl(1 + \lambda\cos(\delta + \tfrac{2\pi k}{3})\bigr), \qquad \delta = \chi \ \ (\sigma_{-1,-1}), \qquad \delta = \chi - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\ \ (\sigma_{-1,1}),
\]
the second with the singlet coordinate oriented by $-I_4 \mapsto +1$; the opposite orientation gives $\chi + \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ up to an overall sign, with the same $Q$.
\item[(iv)] On either projection $Q_{p} = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{\lambda^{2}}{6}$, so the projected vector is null for the equal-coefficient member (the Koide relation $Q = \tfrac23$) if and only if $\lambda^{2} = 2$; equivalently $\|v\|^{2} = 3|C(v)|$; equivalently $|a \cdot a| = \tfrac13|a|^{2}$ for the family vector $a$ of the pairing $[a]_{\times}$; equivalently the Hermitian weights of $v$ on the singlet and the doublet stand in the ratio $1:2$ of their dimensions. At the universal point $\lambda = 1$, $Q_{p} = \tfrac12$.
\end{enumerate}
So on the coherent vector the real-structure question and the Koide number decouple: the choice of structure moves only the phase $\delta$ by a quarter turn (up to the slice's orientation), never $Q$; and if the projected coherent vector is read as the $\sqrt{m}$ vector, the one number of Proposition \claimref{families.chart-computation-sign-twist-bracket-form}(3) becomes the feeding ratio $\lambda^{2} = 2$, which the Gaussian class leaves free.
synthesis.coherent-face-vector-real-slic.technical:
The Gaussian freezing gives a definite complex face vector, $v \propto u' + \lambda e^{I_4\chi}f_{+}$ (numbers read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$): a democratic part and a doublet part on one Fourier line, with $\lambda$ the feeding ratio of the two channels and $\chi$ their relative phase. The real structures of face space that respect the permutation symmetry are $(xP_{s} + yP_{d})$ composed with complex conjugation, and those compatible with the bracket form have $x, y = \pm 1$; two of them make the bracket form the Lorentzian member in which Koide is a nullity statement.

The coherent vector never lies on any of these real slices, for any phase or ratio, because its doublet part sits on a null Fourier line that contains no real direction. Projecting onto a slice is possible, and because that line is null, every projection keeps exactly half the doublet's norm. On the two slices that keep the democratic part, the projected vector has Koide ratio $\tfrac13 + \lambda^{2}/6$ and Koide phase $\chi$ or $\chi - \pi/2$. If the projected coherent vector is read as the vector of square-root masses (a reading, distinct from the skeleton theorem's reading of masses from the spectrum of the mass form), the Koide relation is therefore $\lambda^{2} = 2$, a statement about the channel feeding ratio (equivalently $\|v\|^{2} = 3|C(v)|$, or a $1:2$ split of the norm by dimension), and the choice between the Euclidean and Lorentzian slice only shifts the phase by a quarter turn, up to the slice's orientation.
synthesis.coherent-face-vector-real-slic.lay: The families paper writes the three family masses as a vector and notes that the Koide relation says this vector lies on a light cone, if lengths are measured in a particular relativistic way that the framework does not force. A suggestion was that the framework's own vacuum might supply the missing ingredient, a phase that would put the physical vector on that light cone automatically. This result checks the suggestion against the vector the vacuum actually produces and finds that it fails: that vector never lies in any of the allowed real slices. What can be done is to project it onto one, and then every allowed choice gives the same answer for the Koide ratio, so the choice of geometry carries no information about Koide. If that projected vector is taken to be the physical one, which is a reading and not something shown here, the relation turns into a single condition on how strongly the vacuum's two pairing channels are fed: one must be fed twice as strongly as the other, and nothing in the present theory fixes that.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} An antilinear map commuting with the face action is $A \circ \overline{\phantom{v}}$ with $A$ commuting with every permutation matrix $P$ (the sign of the twist $-P$ cancels on both sides), since the permutation matrices are real. The face representation is $\mathrm{sgn} \oplus \mathbf{2}$ up to the twist, two inequivalent irreducibles each of multiplicity one, so by Schur's lemma $A = xP_{s} + yP_{d}$ with $x, y \in \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$. As $P_{s}$, $P_{d}$ are real projectors, $\sigma^{2}v = A\bar{A}v = (|x|^{2}P_{s} + |y|^{2}P_{d})v$, so $\sigma$ is an involution exactly when $|x| = |y| = 1$. Compatibility: $C(\sigma v) = \bar{v}^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}A\bar{v}$ and $A^{\mathsf{T}}A = x^{2}P_{s} + y^{2}P_{d}$, which equals $1$ exactly when $x^{2} = y^{2} = 1$. The fixed slice of $\sigma_{1,-1}$ is $\{tu + I_4 d : t \in \R,\ d \text{ real doublet}\}$ with $u = u'/\sqrt3$, on which $C = t^{2} - Q(d)$ since $C(u, d) = 0$; that of $\sigma_{-1,1}$ is $\{I_4 tu + d\}$, on which $C = -(t^{2} - Q(d))$; the other two have $C = \pm(t^{2} + Q(d))$, Euclidean.

\emph{(ii)} $P_{s}(e v) = e\kappa u'$ and $P_{d}(e v) = e\kappa w f_{+}$ for nonzero $e \in \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, since $f_{+} \perp u'$ ($\sum_{k}\zeta^{k} = 0$). If $ev$ were fixed by $\sigma_{x,y}$, its doublet part $d$ would satisfy $d = y\bar{d}$, so $d_{k}\bar{d}_{0} = y\bar{d}_{k}\bar{d}_{0}$ and, with $d_{0} = e\kappa w \neq 0$ (as $\lambda > 0$), $d_{1}/d_{0} = \overline{d_{1}/d_{0}}$ would be real. But $d_{1}/d_{0} = \zeta \notin \R$. The line $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}\,f_{+}$ is $C$-null by Proposition \claimref{families.chart-computation-sign-twist-bracket-form}(2), which also records that it contains no nonzero real vector; the argument above is the stronger statement that it contains no complex multiple of one.

\emph{(iii)} The doublet part of $\tfrac12(v + \sigma_{x,y}v)$ is $\tfrac12(D + y\bar{D})$ with $D = \kappa w f_{+}$. Writing $y = \eta^{2}$, $|\eta| = 1$, this is $\eta\,\mathrm{Re}(\bar\eta D)$, of Euclidean square $\sum_{k}\mathrm{Re}(\bar\eta D_{k})^{2} = \tfrac12\bigl(\|D\|^{2} + \mathrm{Re}(\bar\eta^{2}C(D))\bigr) = \tfrac12\|D\|^{2}$, because $C(D) = \kappa^{2}w^{2}C(f_{+}) = 0$; and $\|D\|^{2} = |\kappa|^{2}\lambda^{2}\|f_{+}\|^{2} = 3|\kappa|^{2}\lambda^{2}$. For $\kappa = -I_4|\kappa|$ the singlet $\kappa u'$ is fixed exactly when $x\bar\kappa = \kappa$, that is $x = -1$; among the $C$-compatible structures that leaves $\sigma_{-1,\mp1}$. For $\sigma_{-1,-1}$ the slice is $I_4\R^{3}$ and the real coordinate is $I_4 p$: $I_4 p_{k} = |\kappa|\bigl(1 + \mathrm{Re}(w\zeta^{k})\bigr) = |\kappa|\bigl(1 + \lambda\cos(\chi + 2\pi k/3)\bigr)$. For $\sigma_{-1,1}$ the doublet is kept real and the singlet imaginary, and the real coordinates are $|\kappa|\bigl(1 + \mathrm{Re}(-I_4 w\zeta^{k})\bigr) = |\kappa|\bigl(1 + \lambda\sin(\chi + 2\pi k/3)\bigr) = |\kappa|\bigl(1 + \lambda\cos(\chi - \pi/2 + 2\pi k/3)\bigr)$, with the singlet coordinate oriented by $-I_4 \mapsto +1$; orienting it by $-I_4 \mapsto -1$ multiplies the real coordinates by $-1$ on the singlet only, which, after an overall sign, is $\chi \mapsto \chi + \pi$ on the doublet, that is $\delta = \chi + \pi/2$; $Q$ is unchanged. The restriction of $C$ is (i).

\emph{(iv)} By Proposition \claimref{families.koide-nullity-condition-one-member-invariant}, $Q_{p} = |p|^{2}/(3s^{2})$ with $s = p \cdot u$. Here $s^{2} = 3|\kappa|^{2}$ and, by (iii), $|p|^{2} = s^{2} + Q(d) = 3|\kappa|^{2} + \tfrac32|\kappa|^{2}\lambda^{2}$, so $Q_{p} = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{\lambda^{2}}{6}$, and $Q_{p} = \tfrac23 \iff \lambda^{2} = 2 \iff s^{2} = Q(d)$, the nullity of that Proposition. The equivalent forms: $C(v) = \kappa^{2}\bigl(C(u') + 2wC(u', f_{+}) + w^{2}C(f_{+})\bigr) = 3\kappa^{2}$ and $\|v\|^{2} = 3|\kappa|^{2}(1 + \lambda^{2})$, so $\|v\|^{2} = 3|C(v)| \iff \lambda^{2} = 2$; the Hermitian weights are $\|P_{s}v\|^{2} = 3|\kappa|^{2}$ and $\|P_{d}v\|^{2} = 3|\kappa|^{2}\lambda^{2}$, in ratio $1:2$ exactly then. For the pairing vector of Proposition \claimref{families.rigidity-pairing-sector-one-event}, $a = a_{A} + \lambda e^{I_4\chi}a_{B}$ with $a_{A} = -I_4 u'/\sqrt3$ and $a_{B} = -I_4 f_{+}/\sqrt3$: $a \cdot a = -\tfrac13\bigl(3 + 0 + 0\bigr) = -1$ and $|a|^{2} = 1 + \lambda^{2}$, so $|a \cdot a| = \tfrac13|a|^{2} \iff \lambda^{2} = 2$. At $\lambda = 1$, $Q_{p} = \tfrac12$.

The script verifies, in exact arithmetic in $\Q(\sqrt3)[I_4]$: the isotropy of the Fourier lines and the half-norm of every real slice of $f_{+}$ at rational points of the unit circle; that each $\sigma_{x,y}$ at those points is an equivariant involution, compatible with $C$ exactly at $x, y = \pm1$, the signature of $C$ on a rational basis of each of the four compatible slices ($(3,0)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $(0,3)$ for $(x,y) = (1,1), (1,-1), (-1,1), (-1,-1)$), and fixes no multiple of $v$ for seven values of $w$; the projections, their real coordinates and the value of $Q_{p}$ for those $w$; and the Koide instance $w = 1 + I_4$ ($\lambda^{2} = 2$, $\chi = \pi/4$), where the Lorentzian projection is exactly $C$-null and $\|v\|^{2} = 3|C(v)| = 9$.

synthesis.cumulants-at-fixed-second-mome.formal:
Let $\hat\Omega_{k}$ and $H(\psi)$ be the face operators and mass form of Theorem \claimref{families.skeleton-rank-one-plus-ordering-shift}, with the decomposition $H = \mathbb{1} + \bar\omega\omega^{\mathsf{T}} + K + 2\mathcal{N}$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.face-mass-form-unit-plus-gram}(iii), and let $\rho_{kl} = \sum_{A}\langle a_{kA}^{\dagger}a_{lA}\rangle$ be the one-body family density, $n = \tr\rho$ the mean number of face quanta.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] (The number Gram is the family density.) $\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l} = \tfrac14\bigl(\delta_{kl}\mathbb{1} - e_{l}e_{k}^{\mathsf{T}} \otimes \mathbb{1}\bigr)$ on the six modes, so in every state $2\mathcal{N} = \tfrac12(n\mathbb{1} - \rho^{\mathsf{T}})$. Hence $H \ge \mathbb{1} + \tfrac12(n\mathbb{1} - \rho^{\mathsf{T}})$ and the lightest family has $\lambda_{\min}(H) \ge 1 + \tfrac12(n - \rho_{\max})$, $\rho_{\max}$ the largest eigenvalue of $\rho$: half the population outside the most occupied family direction. In the skeleton $n = 4x$ and $\rho^{\mathsf{T}} = 2x(\mathbb{1} - P_{[\bar v]})$, and the light floor $\cosh^{2}r = 1 + x$ is this bound with equality.
\item[(ii)] (The floor survives every cumulant.) Let $\psi$ be any state, Gaussian or not, whose one- and two-point functions $\langle a_{p}\rangle$, $\langle a_{p}a_{q}\rangle$, $\langle a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}\rangle$ are those of the skeleton at depth $x$. Then $\omega$ and $\mathcal{N}$ are the skeleton's, and
\[
H(\psi) \;=\; (1 + x)\,\mathbb{1} \;+\; (5x + 4x^{2})\,P_{[\bar v]} \;+\; K(\psi), \qquad K(\psi) \ge 0,
\]
so $H(\psi) \ge \cosh^{2}r\,\mathbb{1}$: no family lies below the skeleton's floor, and connected cumulants of any order can only raise masses. The Gaussian value $K = 2x^{2}P_{[\bar v]}$ is one point of the cone $K \ge 0$.
\item[(iii)] (What reaching the data then costs.) Reading $H$'s eigenvalues as masses squared (the skeleton theorem's reading), reproducing $(m_{e}, m_{\mu}, m_{\tau})$ with second moments held at the Koide depth $x^{*} = 769.3325$ (Proposition \claimref{families.koide-class-crossing-fit-conclusion}) needs $\lambda_{\tau} \ge (m_{\tau}/m_{e})^{2}(1 + x^{*}) > 9.31 \times 10^{9}$, against the skeleton's $1 + 6x^{*} + 6x^{*2} < 3.56 \times 10^{6}$, so by Weyl's inequality the largest eigenvalue of $K$ must exceed $\lambda_{\tau} - (1 + 6x^{*} + 4x^{*2})$, more than $7{,}860$ times the Gaussian $2x^{*2}$; and since $\lambda_{\mu} \ge (m_{\mu}/m_{e})^{2}(1 + x^{*})$, the second eigenvalue of $K$, zero in the skeleton, must exceed $\lambda_{\mu} - (1 + 6x^{*} + 4x^{*2}) > 3.05 \times 10^{7}$: the connected Gram matrix must acquire rank two at that size.
\end{enumerate}
So the problem's first route, adding the lowest non-Gaussian cumulant to the frozen vacuum with the skeleton held fixed, cannot reach the charged-lepton spectrum as a correction: the electron cannot be brought below the floor, which is a second-moment quantity (by (i), the population outside the dominant family direction), and the muon and tau must be raised by connected fluctuations thousands of times the Gaussian ones. A completion must instead change the second moments, concentrating the face quanta in the electron's family direction, which within the displaced-Gaussian class with free means is the relabelling of Proposition \claimref{families.classification-displaced-gaussian-class-solved-level}(3); the non-Gaussian structure is needed to cause that concentration, not to add on top of it.
synthesis.cumulants-at-fixed-second-mome.technical:
The mass form of the face modes splits into the unit, the outer square of the coherent vector, a connected Gram matrix $K$ and a number Gram matrix $\mathcal{N}$. This result first identifies $2\mathcal{N}$ exactly: it is $\tfrac12(n\mathbb{1} - \rho^{\mathsf{T}})$, built from the one-body family density $\rho$ alone. So every family's mass squared is at least one plus half the number of quanta sitting outside that family's direction, and the lightest at least one plus half the population outside the most occupied direction. The skeleton's light floor $\cosh^{2}r$ is exactly this bound: its two light directions each hold $2x$ quanta, the heavy one none.

Second, fix the first and second moments at the skeleton's and add any higher connected cumulants. The coherent vector and the number Gram, both second-moment objects, stay put, and only $K$ moves, within the cone of positive semidefinite matrices. So the mass form never drops below $\cosh^{2}r$ times the unit: higher cumulants only raise masses.

With the masses read as square roots of the eigenvalues, the electron would then sit at least at the floor, and the measured ratios force the tau's eigenvalue above $9.3 \times 10^{9}$ at the Koide depth, about $2{,}600$ times the skeleton's, with the connected Gram matrix's top eigenvalue nearly eight thousand times its Gaussian size and a second eigenvalue above $3 \times 10^{7}$ where the skeleton has none. Adding the lowest cumulant is therefore not a perturbative route to the $207$; a completion has to move the second moments, putting the quanta in the electron's direction.
synthesis.cumulants-at-fixed-second-mome.lay: In the series the three charged-lepton families get their masses from a frozen quantum state of six modes, and the simplest (Gaussian) version of that state makes the electron and the muon exactly equally heavy. The open problem asks whether adding a small non-Gaussian ingredient could split them by the observed factor of about 207. This result shows that it cannot do so as a small correction. The lighter pair's common mass in the Gaussian state is fixed by how many quanta sit in the other family directions, and any extra non-Gaussian ingredient that leaves those numbers alone can only make every family heavier, never lighter. Reaching the real masses would then need the extra ingredient to be thousands of times larger than the Gaussian part. What has to change instead is where the quanta sit: almost all of them must be in the electron's direction, and the non-Gaussian structure would have to explain why.

proofs.main:
\emph{Step 1 (the number Gram).} With $\Theta_{k}[(i,A),(j,B)] = \tfrac12\varepsilon_{kij}\varepsilon_{AB}$ as in Theorem \claimref{families.skeleton-rank-one-plus-ordering-shift}, $\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l} = \tfrac14 (E_{k}E_{l}) \otimes \varepsilon^{2} = -\tfrac14 E_{k}E_{l} \otimes \mathbb{1}$ with $(E_{k})_{ij} = \varepsilon_{kij}$, and $(E_{k}E_{l})_{im} = \sum_{j}\varepsilon_{kij}\varepsilon_{ljm} = \delta_{il}\delta_{km} - \delta_{kl}\delta_{im}$, so $\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l} = \tfrac14(\delta_{kl}\mathbb{1} - e_{l}e_{k}^{\mathsf{T}} \otimes \mathbb{1})$. Then $2\mathcal{N}_{kl} = 2\langle a^{\dagger}\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l}a\rangle = \tfrac12(\delta_{kl}n - \sum_{A}\langle a_{lA}^{\dagger}a_{kA}\rangle) = \tfrac12(\delta_{kl}n - \rho_{lk})$. The check verifies the six-by-six identity for all $k, l$ and the state-level identity on three exact non-Gaussian Fock superpositions. Since $\bar\omega\omega^{\mathsf{T}} \ge 0$ and $K \ge 0$ (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.face-mass-form-unit-plus-gram}(iii)), $H \ge \mathbb{1} + \tfrac12(n\mathbb{1} - \rho^{\mathsf{T}})$, whose least eigenvalue is $1 + \tfrac12(n - \rho_{\max})$ ($\rho^{\mathsf{T}}$ has the eigenvalues of $\rho$). In the skeleton, by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.face-mass-form-unit-plus-gram}(iii), $2\mathcal{N} = x(\mathbb{1} + P)$ with $P = P_{[\bar v]}$; comparing traces, $\tfrac12(3n - n) = 4x$, so $n = 4x$ and $\rho^{\mathsf{T}} = n\mathbb{1} - 2x(\mathbb{1} + P) = 2x(\mathbb{1} - P)$, with eigenvalues $2x, 2x, 0$: the heavy direction is empty and the bound is $1 + \tfrac12(4x - 2x) = 1 + x = \cosh^{2}r$, the light eigenvalue of the theorem. This is (i).

\emph{Step 2 (fixed second moments).} $\omega_{k} = \sum_{pq}\Theta_{k}[p,q]\langle a_{p}a_{q}\rangle$ and $\mathcal{N}_{kl} = \sum_{pq}(\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l})[p,q]\langle a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}\rangle$ depend only on the second moments, so for $\psi$ with the skeleton's one- and two-point functions they take the skeleton's values. In the skeleton, by the theorem, $\bar\omega\omega^{\mathsf{T}} + K + 2\mathcal{N} = H - \mathbb{1} = x\mathbb{1} + x(5 + 6x)P$, and by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.face-mass-form-unit-plus-gram}(iii) $K = 2x^{2}P$ and $2\mathcal{N} = x(\mathbb{1} + P)$; so $\bar\omega\omega^{\mathsf{T}} = (x(5 + 6x) - 2x^{2} - x)P = 4x(1 + x)P$ (the check verifies the polynomial identity and the trace identity $\tr H = 3 + n + \sum_{k}\|\hat\Omega_{k}\psi\|^{2}$ at the skeleton). Hence for $\psi$: $H(\psi) = \mathbb{1} + 4x(1 + x)P + K(\psi) + x(\mathbb{1} + P) = (1 + x)\mathbb{1} + (5x + 4x^{2})P + K(\psi)$, with $K(\psi) \ge 0$ because it is the Gram matrix of the vectors $(\hat\Omega_{k} - \omega_{k})\psi$. The last two terms are positive semidefinite, so $H(\psi) - (1 + x)\mathbb{1} \ge 0$; the check confirms the principal-minor criterion on sample Gram matrices. Connected cumulants of every order (and products of the mean with third cumulants, when the state is displaced) enter only through $K$. This is (ii).

\emph{Step 3 (the cost, mass-squared reading).} By clause 2 of the theorem the eigenvalues of $H$ are masses squared. If $\psi$ is as in Step 2 and reproduces the charged-lepton ratios, $\lambda_{e} \ge 1 + x$ and $\lambda_{\tau} = (m_{\tau}/m_{e})^{2}\lambda_{e} \ge (m_{\tau}/m_{e})^{2}(1 + x)$. With $m_{e} = 0.51099895$ MeV, $m_{\mu} = 105.6583755$ MeV and $m_{\tau} \in (1776.84, 1777.02)$ MeV (the store's PDG 2024 values), $(m_{\tau}/m_{e})^{2} \in (1.2090, 1.2094) \times 10^{7}$ and $(m_{\mu}/m_{e})^{2} \in (42753.0, 42753.2)$. At $x^{*} \in (769.3324, 769.3326)$ (Proposition \claimref{families.koide-class-crossing-fit-conclusion}) this gives $\lambda_{\tau} > 9.313 \times 10^{9}$, while $1 + 6x^{*} + 6x^{*2} < 3.556 \times 10^{6}$. Write $A = (1 + x)\mathbb{1} + (5x + 4x^{2})P$, with eigenvalues $1 + 6x + 4x^{2}, 1 + x, 1 + x$. Weyl's inequalities $\lambda_{i + j - 1}(A + K) \le \lambda_{i}(A) + \lambda_{j}(K)$ (eigenvalues in decreasing order) give $\lambda_{1}(K) \ge \lambda_{\tau} - (1 + 6x + 4x^{2})$ and $\lambda_{2}(K) \ge \lambda_{\mu} - (1 + 6x + 4x^{2})$. With $\lambda_{\tau} > 9.313 \times 10^{9}$ the first exceeds $7{,}860 \cdot 2x^{*2}$, and with $\lambda_{\mu} \ge (m_{\mu}/m_{e})^{2}(1 + x^{*})$ the second exceeds $3.05 \times 10^{7}$, where the skeleton's $K = 2x^{2}P$ has rank one (the check brackets all of these exactly). Neither is a correction to the skeleton. This is (iii).

\emph{Scope.} The statement is kinematic and exact. It fixes the second moments at the skeleton's; it does not exclude completions that move the second moments, and by (i) such a completion lowers the electron below $\cosh^{2}r$ only by concentrating the face quanta in one family direction, the electron's. Within the displaced-Gaussian class, free means achieve such a concentration only as the relabelling of Proposition \claimref{families.classification-displaced-gaussian-class-solved-level}(3). The mass-squared reading of $H$ is the skeleton theorem's; under a linear reading the factors in (iii) change but (i) and (ii) do not.

synthesis.face-mass-form-unit-plus-gram.formal:
Let $a_{p}$, $p = (i, A)$, be the six bosonic modes of the face algebra, $\Theta_{k} = \tfrac12(E_{k} \otimes \varepsilon)$ and $\hat\Omega_{k} = \sum_{pq}\Theta_{k}[p,q]\,a_{p}a_{q}$ as in Theorem \claimref{families.skeleton-rank-one-plus-ordering-shift}, and for any state $\psi$ (normalised, with finite fourth moments) let $H_{kl} = \tfrac12\langle\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}\hat\Omega_{l} + \hat\Omega_{l}\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}\rangle$ be that theorem's mass form. For $c \in \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{3}$ (numbers and the module's complex structure are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, the module read on the tower's floors, where $I_4$ commutes with the tower vectors) put $\Theta(c) = \sum_{k}c_{k}\Theta_{k}$ and $\hat\Omega(c) = \sum_{k}c_{k}\hat\Omega_{k}$. Then, for every state, Gaussian or not,
\[
H \;=\; \mathbb{1} \;+\; W^{\dagger}W, \qquad W c \;=\; \bigl(\hat\Omega(c)\psi,\ \sqrt2\,(\Theta(c)a)\psi\bigr) \in \mathcal{F} \oplus \mathcal{F}^{6},
\]
a linear map from face space. For a mixed state $\sum_{i}p_{i}|\psi_{i}\rangle\langle\psi_{i}|$ the same holds with $W^{\dagger}W$ replaced by $\sum_{i}p_{i}W_{i}^{\dagger}W_{i}$, again the unit plus a positive semidefinite (Gram) matrix. Explicitly $H_{kl} = \delta_{kl} + \langle\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}\hat\Omega_{l}\rangle + 2\langle a^{\dagger}\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l}a\rangle$. Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $H \ge \mathbb{1}$: every family's eigenvalue is at least the bare ordering floor $1$, with equality along $c$ exactly when $\hat\Omega(c)\psi = 0$ and $(\Theta(c)a)\psi = 0$.
\item[(ii)] The floor is the identity, invariant under every unitary of face space; all family dependence of $H$, and in particular every splitting of the light pair, lies in $H - \mathbb{1} = W^{\dagger}W$, the Gram matrix of the explicit state vectors $\hat\Omega_{k}\psi$ and $(\Theta_{k}a)\psi$. (That $H - \mathbb{1}$ admits some Gram representation follows from (i) alone; the content here is the bound and the realising vectors.)
\item[(iii)] Splitting the normal-ordered part by the coherent vector $\omega_{k} = \langle\hat\Omega_{k}\rangle$, $W^{\dagger}W = \bar\omega\omega^{\mathsf{T}} + K + 2\mathcal{N}$ with $K_{kl} = \langle(\hat\Omega_{k} - \omega_{k})^{\dagger}(\hat\Omega_{l} - \omega_{l})\rangle$ and $\mathcal{N}_{kl} = \langle a^{\dagger}\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l}a\rangle$, each a Gram matrix: the rank-one outer square of the source plus a connected Gram part plus a number Gram part. In the Gaussian class $K = 2x^{2}P_{[\bar v]}$ and $2\mathcal{N} = x(\mathbb{1} + P_{[\bar v]})$, both along the coherent ray or family-blind, which is why the light pair stays degenerate there.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.face-mass-form-unit-plus-gram.technical:
The families paper's mass form, the symmetrised second moment of the three face operators, was evaluated in closed form only for Gaussian frozen vacua. This result treats every state of the six bosonic face modes. The canonical commutation relations split the symmetrised form into a constant unit matrix, the bare ordering floor, plus the Gram matrix of a linear map from face space into (two copies of) Fock space: one component is the face operator applied to the state, the other the pair operator's one-mode part.

So every family's mass-squared in these units is at least one in every state; the floor is identical for the three families and cannot distinguish them; and all family structure, including any splitting of the electron and muon, sits in the excess over the unit, the Gram matrix of explicit state vectors (any positive semidefinite excess has some Gram form; what is new is the bound and these vectors). That Gram square decomposes further into the outer square of the coherent vector (the democratic source term), a connected part and a number part; in the Gaussian class the last two are aligned with the coherent ray or family-blind, which is the mechanism behind the exact light-pair degeneracy there.
synthesis.face-mass-form-unit-plus-gram.lay: In the families paper the masses of the three generations come from how the vacuum fluctuates in three directions of an internal space. That paper computed this only for the simplest class of vacua, the Gaussian ones, where two generations come out exactly equal. This result looks at every possible vacuum and shows the mass pattern always has the same two-part shape: a fixed baseline, equal for all three generations, plus a part built as the square of something the vacuum determines. So any proposal to separate the electron from the muon has to do it entirely through that second part; the baseline can never help.

proofs.main:
The modes are bosonic (Fact \claimref{families.imported-squeezed-vacuum-bosonic-pairing}), $[a_{p}, a_{q}^{\dagger}] = \delta_{pq}$. Fix $c \in \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{3}$ and write $\Theta = \Theta(c)$, a complex symmetric $6 \times 6$ matrix since each $\Theta_{k}$ is real symmetric, and $\hat\Omega = \hat\Omega(c) = \sum_{pq}\Theta_{pq}a_{p}a_{q}$, so $\hat\Omega^{\dagger} = \sum_{rs}\bar\Theta_{rs}a_{s}^{\dagger}a_{r}^{\dagger}$. From $[a_{p}a_{q}, a_{s}^{\dagger}a_{r}^{\dagger}] = \delta_{qs}\delta_{pr} + \delta_{qr}\delta_{ps} + \delta_{pr}a_{s}^{\dagger}a_{q} + \delta_{ps}a_{r}^{\dagger}a_{q} + \delta_{qr}a_{s}^{\dagger}a_{p} + \delta_{qs}a_{r}^{\dagger}a_{p}$ and the symmetry of $\Theta$,
\[
[\hat\Omega, \hat\Omega^{\dagger}] \;=\; 2\,\mathrm{tr}(\Theta\bar\Theta) \;+\; 4\,a^{\dagger}\,\Theta^{\dagger}\Theta\,a ,
\]
with $a^{\dagger}Xa = \sum_{pq}a_{p}^{\dagger}X_{pq}a_{q}$. Now $\mathrm{tr}(\Theta\bar\Theta) = \sum_{kl}c_{k}\bar{c}_{l}\,\mathrm{tr}(\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l}) = |c|^{2}$, because $\mathrm{tr}(\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l}) = \tfrac14\mathrm{tr}(E_{k}E_{l})\,\mathrm{tr}(\varepsilon\varepsilon) = \delta_{kl}$ (Theorem \claimref{families.skeleton-rank-one-plus-ordering-shift}, proof), and $\langle a^{\dagger}\Theta^{\dagger}\Theta a\rangle = \sum_{p}\|(\Theta a)_{p}\psi\|^{2}$ with $(\Theta a)_{p} = \sum_{q}\Theta_{pq}a_{q}$. Contracting the mass form with $c$,
\[
\bar{c}^{\mathsf{T}}Hc \;=\; \tfrac12\bigl\langle\hat\Omega^{\dagger}\hat\Omega + \hat\Omega\hat\Omega^{\dagger}\bigr\rangle
\;=\; \langle\hat\Omega^{\dagger}\hat\Omega\rangle + \tfrac12\bigl\langle[\hat\Omega, \hat\Omega^{\dagger}]\bigr\rangle
\;=\; |c|^{2} + \|\hat\Omega\psi\|^{2} + 2\sum_{p}\|(\Theta a)_{p}\psi\|^{2} \;=\; |c|^{2} + \|Wc\|^{2},
\]
using $\sum_{kl}\bar{c}_{k}\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}\hat\Omega_{l}c_{l} = \hat\Omega(c)^{\dagger}\hat\Omega(c)$ and $\sum_{kl}\bar{c}_{k}\hat\Omega_{l}\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}c_{l} = \hat\Omega(c)\hat\Omega(c)^{\dagger}$. Since $W$ is linear in $c$, polarisation gives $H = \mathbb{1} + W^{\dagger}W$, whose entries are the displayed $\delta_{kl} + \langle\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}\hat\Omega_{l}\rangle + 2\langle a^{\dagger}\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l}a\rangle$ (the $\Theta_{k}$ being real). Mixed states follow by linearity of $H$ in the state, $H = \sum_{i}p_{i}(\mathbb{1} + W_{i}^{\dagger}W_{i})$. (i) and (ii) are immediate: $\bar{c}^{\mathsf{T}}(H - \mathbb{1})c = \|Wc\|^{2} \ge 0$, vanishing exactly when both components of $Wc$ vanish, and the identity commutes with every unitary of face space. (iii): $\hat\Omega_{k}\psi = \omega_{k}\psi + (\hat\Omega_{k} - \omega_{k})\psi$ with the second vector orthogonal to $\psi$, so $\langle\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}\hat\Omega_{l}\rangle = \bar\omega_{k}\omega_{l} + K_{kl}$, and $K$ and $\mathcal{N}$ are Gram matrices of the vectors $(\hat\Omega_{l} - \omega_{l})\psi$ and $((\Theta_{l}a)_{p}\psi)_{p}$. In the Gaussian class the theorem's computation gives $\langle\hat\Omega_{k}^{\dagger}\hat\Omega_{l}\rangle = 2x(2 + 3x)\bar{n}_{k}n_{l}$ and $\bar\omega_{k}\omega_{l} = 4x(1 + x)\bar{n}_{k}n_{l}$, so $K = 2x^{2}P_{[\bar v]}$, and its ordering term $c^{2}\delta_{kl} + x\bar{n}_{k}n_{l} = \delta_{kl} + 2\mathcal{N}_{kl}$ gives $2\mathcal{N} = x(\mathbb{1} + P_{[\bar v]})$.

The script works in the unnormalised monomial basis of the Fock space, where every amplitude is a complex rational: it checks $\mathrm{tr}(\Theta_{k}\Theta_{l}) = \delta_{kl}$ and the symmetry of $\Theta_{k}$, and verifies $H_{kl} = \langle\psi|\psi\rangle\delta_{kl} + \langle\hat\Omega_{k}\psi, \hat\Omega_{l}\psi\rangle + 2\sum_{p}\langle(\Theta_{k}a)_{p}\psi, (\Theta_{l}a)_{p}\psi\rangle$ entry by entry, exactly, on four states including non-Gaussian superpositions of up to five monomials with complex rational coefficients.

synthesis.faces-of-one-slot-space-are-no.technical:
Read the three faces of the three-spinor composite inside one state space $V = \Lambda^{\bullet}(S \oplus W)$, $S = \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{3}$ the slots, the face-$F$ copy being $V_{F} = \Lambda^{\bullet}(S_{F} \oplus W)$ under Hypothesis (S). The robust statement is the gauge-group one: any Lie algebra acting linearly on $S$ leaves at most one face plane irreducible, since two distinct face planes meet in a slot line that would be invariant in both; so at most one face is a weak doublet, and under the weak group of face $\{1,2\}$ the other faces' halves are not invariant. It holds whatever the pair modes.

The faces' chirality halves also overlap. With chirality the mode-number parity and one pair system shared by the faces they span $28$ of the $32$ even states (the four slot-free states common to all three faces, the one-slot states shared pairwise, only the two-slot states face-specific), at most $40$ with halves chosen face by face; with separate pair modes per face they span $46$, at most $47$; in every case fewer than the $48$ of three generations. With shared slots the faces are not three generations under one gauge group; the identification needs three composites with separate slots.
synthesis.faces-of-one-slot-space-are-no.lay: One proposal in the series says the three families of matter particles are the three ways of choosing two of the three building blocks of a largest composite. In a quantum field theory, three families means three separate copies of the particle content, all feeling the same forces in the same way. If the three choices live in one shared set of states, this fails twice: the weak force can treat only one of the three pairs as a doublet, because any two pairs share a block, and the shared blocks make the copies overlap, giving at most 28 distinct states (46 if each pair keeps its own colour modes) where three families need 48. The idea survives only if the three pairs are three separate composites.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} The face-$F$ copy of Theorem \claimref{families.three-identical-families-mixing-shared-slots} is the composite of the two conformal spinors on the slots $F$ with the construction of Hypothesis (S) applied to it; under (S) (Theorem \claimref{standard-model.hyp-s-slot-statistics}) its state space is $\Lambda^{\bullet}(\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{2} \oplus W)$, the slots are fermionic modes, $U(2) \times U(3)$ acts as $\Lambda^{\bullet}(A \oplus B)$, and the chirality is the parity of the mode number. The slot mixing $U(2)$ of a face is the weak group with hypercharge: it acts on the slot coefficients by $\alpha \mapsto X\alpha$ with generators $T_{j} = \tfrac{I_4}{2}\sigma_{j}$ and $Y = \tfrac{I_4}{2}\mathbf{1}$ (slot coefficients, and the entries of $\sigma_{j}$, read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$) (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.rung-field-d-term-action-and-tree-masses-on-the-lift-locus}). The stored theorem says the faces pairwise share exactly one slot; we take that literally, in one state space $V = \Lambda^{\bullet}(S \oplus W)$ with $S = \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{3}$ spanned by the slot modes $s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}$, so that $V_{F} = \Lambda^{\bullet}(S_{F} \oplus W) \subset V$ and two faces share the modes of their common slot. Three generations of a field theory are three copies of the content acted on by one gauge group, with $3 \times 16$ independent one-particle states of each chirality.

\emph{(1).} Let $\mathfrak{g}$ act linearly on $S$ and suppose two distinct face planes $S_{F}$, $S_{G}$ are invariant. They are two distinct planes in a three-dimensional space, so $S_{F} \cap S_{G} = \ell$ is a line (the common slot), and $\ell$ is invariant as an intersection of invariant subspaces. Then $S_{F}$ contains the invariant line $\ell$, so it is not irreducible; likewise $S_{G}$. Hence at most one face plane is an irreducible invariant subspace. If the weak $\su(2)$ acts on the slots, a face whose slots form a weak doublet has an irreducible invariant plane (the doublet), so at most one face does. The script computes, for each pair of faces, the full joint stabiliser $\{X \in \gl(3, \mathbb{Q}) : XS_{F} \subset S_{F}, XS_{G} \subset S_{G}\}$ by exact elimination on the conditions $X(e_{a}) \wedge B_{F} = 0$ ($a \in F$, $B_{F}$ the face blade in $\Cl(3,0)$), finds dimension $5$, and verifies that every basis element preserves both planes and maps the common line into itself; a matrix moving the common line inside $S_{F}$ off $S_{G}$ is outside it, and the stabiliser of one plane has dimension $7$ and contains $E_{ab}$, $E_{ba}$, which have no common eigenline in $S_{F}$ (an irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$). The rational computation decides the complex case, since the conditions are linear with rational coefficients. With the weak group of the face $\{1,2\}$, $T_{3} = \tfrac12(n_{1} - n_{2})$ on occupation numbers, the even half of $V_{\{1,2\}}$ has the symmetric multiset $\{-\tfrac12: 4, 0: 8, \tfrac12: 4\}$, while those of $V_{\{1,3\}}$ and $V_{\{2,3\}}$ are $\{0: 8, \tfrac12: 8\}$ and $\{-\tfrac12: 8, 0: 8\}$; the weight multiset of a finite-dimensional $\su(2)$ representation is symmetric under $T_{3} \to -T_{3}$, so these halves are not invariant. The face $\{1,3\}$'s would-be quark doublet $\{s_{1}w, s_{3}w\}$ has $T_{3} = \tfrac12$ and $0$: one member of a weak doublet and one singlet.

\emph{(2).} Take $W = \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{3}$ (the three pair modes of one pair system) and write basis states of $V$ as exterior monomials $s_{A}w_{B}$, $A \subset \{1,2,3\}$, $B \subset \{1,2,3\}$, $64$ in all. $V_{F}$ is spanned by the monomials with $A \subset F$, $32$ of them, $16$ of even mode number. A monomial with $|A| = 0$ lies in all three $V_{F}$, one with $|A| = 1$ in the two faces containing its slot, one with $|A| = 2$ in exactly one face, and $|A| = 3$ in none. By inclusion and exclusion the face modules span $3 \cdot 32 - 3 \cdot 16 + 8 = 56$ states, and the even halves $3 \cdot 16 - 3 \cdot 8 + 4 = 28$ of the $32$ even states: $4$ slot-free states (the colour-neutral vacuum and the three two-pair states, the $\nu^{c}$ and $u^{c}$ of every face in the store's labelling), $12$ one-slot states (each $Q$ and $L$ state shared by the two faces through its slot) and $12$ two-slot states ($e^{c}$ and $d^{c}$, one face each). If the faces are allowed different halves, an even half and an odd half are disjoint and two halves of one parity overlap as above, so the best choice, two faces of one parity and one of the other, gives $16 + 16 - 8 + 16 = 40$. The script builds the $64$ states, computes the spans by exact rank ($56$, $28$, and $40$ as the maximum over all eight choices) and the sharing pattern $\{(0, 3): 4, (1, 2): 12, (2, 1): 12\}$ of (slot number, number of faces).

\emph{(2), separate pair modes.} If each face carries its own pair modes $W_{F} \cong \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{3}$ (nine pair modes in all) while the slots are still shared, a monomial $s_{A}w_{B}$ of face $F$ has $B \subset W_{F}$, so two faces share exactly the monomials with $B = \emptyset$ and $A$ inside both faces: the vacuum (all three faces) and the one-slot states $s_{i}$ (two faces each). The even halves therefore share only the vacuum and span $3 \cdot 16 - 2 = 46$; with halves chosen face by face, two even and one odd give $31 + 16 = 47$, three odd give $48 - 3 = 45$, so the maximum is $47$. The script builds the $2^{12}$ states of this reading and recomputes $46$ and $47$ by exact rank. Either way the count is below $48$.

\emph{(3).} Three generations need $48$ independent one-particle states of one chirality, acted on alike by one gauge group. Whenever the faces share slot modes, (2) gives at most $40$ with one shared pair system ($28$ with the chirality of (S), one $\nu^{c}$ and one $u^{c}$ serving all three faces) and at most $47$ with separate pair modes ($46$ with the chirality of (S), the vacuum shared), so the faces' copies are not independent. And (1) gives at most one face transforming as a generation under any gauge algebra acting on the slots. So in this reading the conjecture \claimref{families.three-generations-faces-maximal-composite} fails as a field-theory statement. What is not excluded is the reading in which each face is a separate two-spinor composite with its own slot modes and pair modes, three copies of $\Lambda^{\bullet}(\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}^{2} \oplus W)$ with one gauge group acting diagonally; there "two faces share one slot" is a correspondence of labels between composites, not a shared mode, and the mixing-by-overlap reading of Theorem \claimref{families.three-identical-families-mixing-shared-slots}, stated there at observation level, has no operator content without a further rule relating the composites. The result is transport-absent: it is linear algebra on the slot module.

synthesis.imported-brannen-charged-lepto.formal:
Brannen writes the square roots of the three charged-lepton masses as the eigenvalues of a $3 \times 3$ circulant,
\[
\sqrt{m_{n}} \;=\; \mu\bigl(1 + 2\eta\cos(\delta + 2n\pi/3)\bigr), \qquad n = 0, 1, 2,
\]
where $\eta^{2} = \tfrac12$ is the Koide relation, and fits $\mu = 17716.13(109)$ eV$^{1/2}$, $\eta^{2} = 0.500003(23)$ and $\delta = 0.2222220(19)$ to the measured masses, observing that $\delta$ is close to $\tfrac29$. This is an empirical fit, not a derivation. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Brannen2006}, equations (4) and (14).
synthesis.imported-brannen-charged-lepto.technical: Koide's relation says that the sum of the three charged-lepton masses is two thirds of the square of the sum of their square roots. Brannen wrote the square roots as the eigenvalues of a circulant matrix, $\mu(1 + \sqrt2\cos(\delta + 2n\pi/3))$ when the Koide relation holds exactly, so that the masses are fixed by a scale $\mu$ and one phase $\delta$. Fitted to the lepton masses, the phase came out as $0.2222220$ with an uncertainty in the seventh decimal place, close to $\tfrac29$; the fit is an observation and no mechanism is given for the value.
synthesis.imported-brannen-charged-lepto.lay: The masses of the electron, muon and tau satisfy a surprisingly precise numerical relation found by Koide. Brannen noticed that, written in a natural way, the relation leaves one angle free, and that the measured masses make that angle very close to two ninths. Whether that closeness means anything is not known.

imported_from.citation: C. A. Brannen, The lepton masses, preprint, 2 May 2006, brannenworks.com/MASSWS2.pdf, equations (4) and (14).

synthesis.imported-flag-2024-light-quark.formal: The FLAG 2024 averages of lattice QCD results (Table 1; quark masses in the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme at $2$ GeV) are, for $N_{f} = 2+1+1$: $m_{ud} = 3.427(51)$ MeV, $m_{s} = 93.46(58)$ MeV, $m_{s}/m_{ud} = 27.227(81)$, $m_{u}/m_{d} = 0.465(24)$, $m_{c}/m_{s} = 11.766(30)$; and for $N_{f} = 2+1$ (three dynamical flavours, a different lattice average, hence a strange mass below the stored quantity.strange-quark-mass): $m_{ud} = 3.387(39)$ MeV, a strange mass of $92.4(1.0)$ MeV, $m_{s}/m_{ud} = 27.42(12)$, $m_{u}/m_{d} = 0.485(19)$, $m_{c}/m_{s} = 11.82(16)$, with $m_{ud} = (m_{u} + m_{d})/2$. The ratios are scale independent in QCD. At the $N_{f} = 2+1+1$ central values $m_{s}/m_{d} = \tfrac12(m_{s}/m_{ud})(1 + m_{u}/m_{d}) \approx 19.94$ and $m_{c}/m_{u} \approx 505$; at the $N_{f} = 2+1$ central values about $20.36$ and $496$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{FLAG2024} (Table 1).
synthesis.imported-flag-2024-light-quark.technical: The Flavour Lattice Averaging Group reviews lattice QCD computations and quotes world averages. Its 2024 averages of the light-quark mass ratios, with and without a dynamical charm quark, fix the ratios of the down to the strange and of the up to the charm mass to a few percent, more precisely than the individual running masses.
synthesis.imported-flag-2024-light-quark.lay: The masses of the light quarks cannot be weighed directly; they are computed by large simulations of the strong force on a lattice. The FLAG review collects and averages these computations; its ratios of quark masses are the most precise available.

imported_from.citation: Y. Aoki et al. (Flavour Lattice Averaging Group), FLAG Review 2024, arXiv:2411.04268.

synthesis.imported-flavour-blind-quark-m.technical: Quark masses are not fixed numbers in quantum chromodynamics: they depend on the energy scale at which they are defined, and they change at the thresholds where a heavier quark stops taking part. In the standard minimal-subtraction scheme both effects treat every quark alike. The rate of running is one function of the strong coupling for all flavours, and at a heavy-quark threshold all lighter masses are matched by one common factor. So, at any common scale, perturbative QCD rescales all quark masses together, and their ratios do not depend on the scale chosen. Electromagnetic and electroweak corrections, which do distinguish flavours, are not part of this statement.
synthesis.imported-flavour-blind-quark-m.lay: The mass of a quark, as physicists define it, changes slowly with the energy at which it is measured, because of the strong force. This standard result says that the strong force changes all the quark masses by the same factor when they are compared at the same energy, so it does not alter how the masses compare with each other.

imported_from.citation: S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Review of Particle Physics, Phys. Rev. D 110 (2024) 030001.

synthesis.imported-fritzsch-texture-cabi.formal:
For quark mass matrices whose light $2 \times 2$ block has the nearest-neighbour (Fritzsch) form, zero in the light-light entry and equal moduli off the diagonal, each sector's light-plane rotation angle obeys $\tan\theta_{u} = \sqrt{m_{u}/m_{c}}$, $\tan\theta_{d} = \sqrt{m_{d}/m_{s}}$ (the Gatto-Sartori-Tonin relation for the texture of Fritzsch), and with $\psi$ the relative phase of the two sectors' off-diagonal entries the Cabibbo element is
\[
\sin\theta_{C} = |R_{u} - R_{d}\,e^{-I_4\psi}|,\qquad
R_{u} = \sqrt{\tfrac{m_{u}}{m_{u} + m_{c}}}\sqrt{\tfrac{m_{s}}{m_{d} + m_{s}}},\quad
R_{d} = \sqrt{\tfrac{m_{c}}{m_{u} + m_{c}}}\sqrt{\tfrac{m_{d}}{m_{d} + m_{s}}},
\]
in the limit where the heavy family decouples; equivalently, with $x = m_{u}/m_{c}$ and $y = m_{d}/m_{s}$, $\sin^{2}\theta_{C} = (x + y - 2\sqrt{xy}\cos\psi)/((1 + x)(1 + y))$. The measured $|V_{us}|$ with the light-quark mass ratios selects $\psi$ near $90^{\circ}$ (about $79^{\circ}$ at the central inputs of 1999, $38^{\circ}$ to $115^{\circ}$ over them). The mass-matrix entries and the phase are numbers, read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ (conventions, the unit principle, U1). \emph{Provenance:} \cite{GST1968}, \cite{Fritzsch1978}, \cite{FritzschXing1999} (eqs. (3.8) to (3.10), Section 5.1).
synthesis.imported-fritzsch-texture-cabi.technical: The oldest successful quark-mass relation says that the Cabibbo angle is about the square root of the down to strange mass ratio. In the nearest-neighbour textures of Fritzsch it holds sector by sector, and the Cabibbo angle is the modulus of the difference of the up-sector and down-sector contributions, which depends on one relative phase. Fritzsch and Xing showed that the data put that phase near a right angle, which also makes the unitarity triangle nearly rectangular.
synthesis.imported-fritzsch-texture-cabi.lay: A classic observation in particle physics links how strongly quarks of different families mix to the ratios of their masses. In one well-known family of models the mixing comes out as the difference of two such square-root ratios, offset by a phase, and the measured mixing wants that phase to be close to a right angle.

imported_from.citation: R. Gatto, G. Sartori and M. Tonin, Weak self-masses, Cabibbo angle, and broken SU(2) x SU(2), Phys. Lett. B 28 (1968), 128--130.
H. Fritzsch, Weak-interaction mixing in the six-quark theory, Phys. Lett. B 73 (1978), 317.
H. Fritzsch and Z.-z. Xing, The light quark sector, CP violation, and the unitarity triangle, Nucl. Phys. B 556 (1999), 49--75; arXiv:hep-ph/9904286.

synthesis.imported-one-loop-pole-mass-re.formal:
For a heavy quark $Q$, the pole mass $M_{Q}$ and the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass at its own scale are related by
\[
M_{Q} = m_{Q}(m_{Q})\Bigl[1 + \frac{4\alpha_{s}(m_{Q})}{3\pi} + O(\alpha_{s}^{2})\Bigr],
\]
so at one loop the pole mass exceeds the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass by the positive fraction $4\alpha_{s}(m_{Q})/3\pi$, which is larger for the lighter of two heavy quarks because $\alpha_{s}$ decreases with the scale. The higher-order terms are of comparable size to the one-loop term at the charm and bottom scales; the series is asymptotic. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{PDG2024} (Review 60, Eq. (60.25)), \cite{Tarrach1981}.
synthesis.imported-one-loop-pole-mass-re.technical: A heavy quark's mass can be defined as the position of the pole of its propagator or as the running mass of the minimal-subtraction scheme taken at its own scale. At one loop in the strong coupling the pole mass is larger, by the fraction $4\alpha_{s}/3\pi$ with the coupling evaluated at the quark's mass. Since the coupling is stronger at lower scales, the correction is relatively larger for charm than for bottom, and for bottom than for top. The higher-order corrections are not small at the charm and bottom scales, so the relation is used at the order stated.
synthesis.imported-one-loop-pole-mass-re.lay: There is more than one way to define the mass of a heavy quark. This standard result relates two common definitions: the so-called pole mass is a little larger than the running mass, by an amount that grows with the strength of the strong force, which is stronger for the lighter heavy quarks.

imported_from.locator: Review 60, Quark masses (R. M. Barnett, L. P. Lellouch and A. V. Manohar), Eq. (60.25)

synthesis.imported-one-loop-qed-pole-mas.formal:
For a charged lepton $i$ of unit charge, the pole mass and the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ running mass at scale $\mu$ are related at one loop in QED by
\[
m_{i}^{\mathrm{pole}} = \Bigl[1 + \frac{\alpha}{\pi}\Bigl\{\frac34\ln\frac{\mu^{2}}{\bar{m}_{i}(\mu)^{2}} + 1\Bigr\}\Bigr]\bar{m}_{i}(\mu),
\]
the QED analogue of the QCD relation of \claimref{synthesis.imported-one-loop-pole-mass-relation} with the colour factor replaced by the squared charge. Since the correction depends on the lepton through $\ln\bar{m}_{i}$, ratios of running masses at a common scale differ from ratios of pole masses at first order in $\alpha$, and Koide's relation, which holds for the pole masses to about $10^{-5}$, would be corrected by about $0.1\%$ if it held for running masses instead. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Sumino2009b} (eq. (6)), \cite{Sumino2009}.
synthesis.imported-one-loop-qed-pole-mas.technical: A charged lepton's mass can be defined as the pole of its propagator or as a running mass in the minimal-subtraction scheme. At one loop in QED the two differ by a fraction of order $\alpha/\pi$ that contains the logarithm of the mass itself, so the electron, muon and tau are shifted by different amounts. Mass ratios, and Koide's relation among the three, therefore depend on which definition is used, at the level of a part in a thousand.
synthesis.imported-one-loop-qed-pole-mas.lay: There are two standard ways to define the mass of a charged particle such as the electron, and quantum effects of electromagnetism make them differ slightly, by different amounts for the electron, muon and tau. A famous exact-looking relation among the three masses holds for one definition and is off by a tenth of a percent for the other.

imported_from.citation: Y. Sumino, Family gauge symmetry as an origin of Koide's mass formula and charged lepton spectrum, arXiv:0903.3640 (2009), report TU-842.
Y. Sumino, Family gauge symmetry as an origin of Koide's mass formula and charged lepton spectrum, J. High Energy Phys. 05 (2009), 075.

synthesis.imported-takagi-factorisation.formal: Let $A$ be a complex $n \times n$ matrix with $A^{\mathsf T} = A$. Then $A = U\Sigma U^{\mathsf T}$ with $U$ unitary and $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}, \dots, \sigma_{n})$ real and nonnegative; the $\sigma_{i}$ are the singular values of $A$, the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A\bar{A} = AA^{\dagger}$, and the columns of $U$ (the Takagi vectors) are orthonormal eigenvectors of $AA^{\dagger}$, fixed up to a sign for a simple nonzero $\sigma_{i}$ and up to a real orthogonal change of basis within a degenerate one. For a symmetric mass matrix $M$ in a Lagrangian term $\tfrac12\psi^{\mathsf T}M\psi$ the masses are the $\sigma_{i}$ and the mass states are the Takagi vectors. Here the complex numbers are those of the imported mass matrices. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Cor.~4.4.4]{HornJohnson}.
synthesis.imported-takagi-factorisation.technical: A complex symmetric matrix, such as a Majorana neutrino mass matrix, is diagonalised not by a unitary similarity but by a unitary congruence, $U^{\mathsf T}$ on one side and $U$ on the other. The diagonal entries can be taken real and nonnegative and are then the singular values. The vectors that do it are eigenvectors of the Hermitian matrix $AA^{\dagger}$; for a real symmetric matrix they are its real eigenvectors, with a factor $i$ on those of negative eigenvalue.
synthesis.imported-takagi-factorisation.lay: A standard theorem of matrix algebra says how to find the masses and the mass states when the masses of neutral particles are described by a symmetric table of complex numbers: the masses are the table's singular values, and the states are found from an associated table that is easier to handle.

imported_from.citation: R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013).

synthesis.koide-channel-phase-is-no-symm.formal:
Read the projected coherent face vector of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.coherent-face-vector-real-slices}(iii)-(iv) as the $\sqrt{m}$ vector (its circulant reading; the mass-squared reading of the mass form is a different dictionary, in which the channel phase does not enter the spectrum of source-built completions by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.real-structure-breaks-source-stabiliser-to-z2}). At the Koide depth $\lambda^{2} = 2$ it is, up to a common factor, $p_{k} = 1 + \sqrt2\cos(\delta + \tfrac{2\pi k}{3})$, $k = 0, 1, 2$, with $\delta$ the channel phase $\chi$ on the Euclidean slice and $\chi \mp \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ on the Lorentzian one; read as the $\sqrt{m}$ vector it satisfies the Koide relation (Proposition \claimref{families.koide-nullity-condition-one-member-invariant}). The relabellings of the three families and the sign of the doublet part act on $\delta$ through $\pm\delta + \tfrac{\pi}{3}\mathbb{Z}$, and $\chi - \delta \in \{0, \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}\}$, so the channel phase lies on the orbit $\pm\delta + \tfrac{\pi}{6}\mathbb{Z}$. Let $r(\delta) = (p_{2}/p_{1})^{2}$ and let $r_{\mathrm{obs}} = m_{\mu}/m_{e}$ at the stored masses, taken in the window $(206.7682690, 206.7682969)$ (three stored standard deviations of $m_{\mu}$; for $m_{e}$, $10^{-9}$ MeV).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The phase target.)} In the fundamental domain $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{6}]$ of $\pm\delta + \tfrac{\pi}{3}\mathbb{Z}$ all three $p_{k}$ are positive exactly on $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{12})$, where $p_{1} < p_{2} < p_{0}$ for $\delta > 0$; there $r$ increases strictly from $1$ to $\infty$, and $r(\delta_{*}) = r_{\mathrm{obs}}$ gives $\delta_{*} \in (0.22222204589, 0.22222204830)$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{($\tfrac29$ is excluded at exact Koide.)} $r(\tfrac29) \in (206.7703, 206.7704)$, above the window by more than $400$ standard deviations of the measured ratio; so $\delta_{*} < \tfrac29 - 1.7 \times 10^{-7}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(No small rational.)} No rational with denominator below $630131$ lies in the window of (i) (a property of the three-standard-deviation window); $\tfrac{140029}{630131}$ is the first.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(No symmetry angle.)} No rational of denominator below $25249$ lies in the corresponding window for $\delta_{*}/\pi$; hence no point of the orbit $\pm\delta_{*} + \tfrac{\pi}{6}\mathbb{Z}$, and so neither the channel phase $\chi$ on either slice nor any relabelling of it, is $\tfrac{a}{b}\pi$ with $b \le 4208$ (again for the three-standard-deviation window).
\item[(v)] \emph{(Elasticity.)} $(\delta/r)\,dr/d\delta \in (12.4, 12.5)$ across the window: the split responds to the phase with elasticity about $12.5$, not the unit elasticity of the relabelling signature of Proposition \claimref{families.classification-displaced-gaussian-class-solved-level}.
\end{enumerate}
So at exact Koide the open problem's $207$ is the single number $\delta_{*}$, known to $2.4 \times 10^{-9}$. A phase fixed by a finite-order symmetry (a root-of-unity condition, the kind every stabiliser met in face space supplies: the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ of the real structure, the $S_{3}$, the doublet quarter-turn, the $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$ of the cubic family word) is a rational multiple of $\pi$ (argued, not proved), and such a phase is excluded by (iv) for symmetries of order up to $4208$; the celebrated value $\tfrac29$ is excluded jointly with exact Koide by (ii). A selection rule for the non-Gaussian frozen vacuum must therefore produce a transcendental-looking phase to about $10^{-9}$, or produce a Koide defect along with it.

\emph{Note (mass definition).} The window, the exclusion of $\tfrac29$ and the denominator bounds use the stored pole masses, which the store's provisional dictionary assigns to the face mass form (note in \claimref{families.skeleton-rank-one-plus-ordering-shift}); exact Koide at pole masses is then a premise of the reading. At common-scale running masses, first order in $\alpha$, the target phase lies between $0.22254$ and $0.22258$, moved from $\delta_{*}$ by more than $1800$ times the distance from $\delta_{*}$ to $\tfrac29$, and $m_{\mu}/m_{e}$ between $210.58$ and $210.89$ (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.koide-channel-phase-target-depends-on-mass-definition}).
synthesis.koide-channel-phase-is-no-symm.technical: Reading the projected coherent face vector as the vector of square roots of the charged-lepton masses (its circulant reading), these are, at the Koide depth, $1 + \sqrt2\cos(\delta + 2\pi k/3)$ with $\delta$ the channel phase of the coherent face source (up to a quarter turn, depending on which real slice is used). So, granted the Koide relation, the muon-to-electron ratio is a function of one phase. This result solves for that phase from the measured muon and electron masses alone, using certified interval arithmetic: $\delta_{*}$ lies between $0.22222204589$ and $0.22222204830$. It then tests the two kinds of value a rule could supply without a second free number. The often-quoted value $2/9$ gives a ratio of $206.7703$ against the measured $206.76828$: excluded by more than $400$ standard deviations when the Koide relation is exact; it is the combination of exact Koide with $2/9$ that fails. Within three standard deviations of the muon mass, no fraction with denominator below $630131$ fits the window, and no rational multiple of $\pi$ with denominator up to $4208$ fits it on any relabelling. Since a phase fixed by a symmetry of finite order is a rational multiple of $\pi$ (argued), this rules out phases produced by symmetries of order up to $4208$, including all the stabilisers met in face space so far. Under the other dictionary, where the eigenvalues of the mass form are the squared masses, the channel phase does not reach the spectrum at all, so the result is specific to the square-root reading. The split's relative response to the phase is certified between $12.4$ and $12.5$ times the phase's relative change, so a rule must fix the phase to within the window's width, $2.4 \times 10^{-9}$, to reproduce the ratio to its measured precision.
synthesis.koide-channel-phase-is-no-symm.lay: A famous formula ties the electron, muon and tau masses together. In one reading of this framework, where a vector built from the vacuum is read as the square roots of the three masses, the remaining information in the masses is a single angle once that formula is granted. This result pins that angle down from the measured electron and muon masses to nine decimal places and checks the two kinds of value a theory might naturally produce. It is not the simple fraction $2/9$ that has been proposed before (close, but measurably different if the formula is exact), not any other fraction with a small denominator, and not the kind of angle a symmetry of modest order would produce, which is a simple fraction of a half-turn. Whatever fixes the muon-to-electron mass ratio has to produce a number that looks like none of these.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} Throughout, the projected coherent vector is read as the $\sqrt{m}$ vector (its circulant reading); every statement below is conditional on that reading. By Proposition \claimref{synthesis.coherent-face-vector-real-slices}(iii) the projected coherent face vector is $p_{k} = |\kappa|(1 + \lambda\cos(\delta + \tfrac{2\pi k}{3}))$ with $\delta = \chi$ on the Euclidean slice and $\delta = \chi \mp \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ on the Lorentzian one (by the orientation of the singlet coordinate), and by (iv) it satisfies the Koide relation exactly when $\lambda^{2} = 2$, which is the null condition of the equal-coefficient member of Proposition \claimref{families.koide-nullity-condition-one-member-invariant}. Drop the common factor and take $\lambda = \sqrt2$. Relabelling the families shifts $\delta$ by multiples of $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$, reflecting the labels sends $\delta \mapsto -\delta$, and reversing the sign of the doublet part shifts $\delta$ by $\pi$; together these generate $\pm\delta + \tfrac{\pi}{3}\mathbb{Z}$, and with the slice choice the channel phase lies on $\pm\delta + \tfrac{\pi}{6}\mathbb{Z}$. Write $c = \cos\delta$, $s = \sin\delta$; then $\cos(\delta + \tfrac{2\pi}{3}) = -\tfrac{c}{2} - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}s$ and $\cos(\delta + \tfrac{4\pi}{3}) = -\tfrac{c}{2} + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}s$, so $r(\delta) = (p_{2}/p_{1})^{2}$ is evaluated without any value of $\pi$.

\emph{(i)} On $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{6}]$, $\delta + \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ runs over $[\tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}]$, where the cosine falls from $-\tfrac12$ to $-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and crosses $-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ at $\delta = \tfrac{\pi}{12}$; so $p_{1} > 0$ exactly for $\delta < \tfrac{\pi}{12}$ (the positive root, as Proposition \claimref{synthesis.light-cone-koide-is-quarter-turn}(iv) selects it). On $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{12}]$, $\delta + \tfrac{4\pi}{3} \in [\tfrac{4\pi}{3}, \tfrac{17\pi}{12}]$, where the cosine rises from $-\tfrac12$, so $p_{2}$ increases and stays above $1 - \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} > 0$, while $p_{1}$ decreases to $0$; hence $r = (p_{2}/p_{1})^{2}$ increases strictly from $1$ (at $\delta = 0$, $p_{1} = p_{2}$) to $\infty$, and $r(\delta) = r_{\mathrm{obs}}$ has exactly one solution there. The check evaluates $r$ in certified interval arithmetic: $\sin$ and $\cos$ of a rational in $(0, 1)$ by Taylor polynomials of degree $47$ with twice the first omitted term as error (the series alternates with decreasing terms), $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ by integer square roots at $10^{-40}$, every interval end rounded outwards to $10^{-40}$. The window for $r_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is $((m_{\mu} - 3\sigma_{\mu})/(m_{e} + \epsilon_{e}), (m_{\mu} + 3\sigma_{\mu})/(m_{e} - \epsilon_{e}))$ at the stored values $m_{\mu} = 105.6583755$ MeV, $\sigma_{\mu} = 2.3 \times 10^{-6}$ MeV, $m_{e} = 0.51099895$ MeV, with $\epsilon_{e} = 10^{-9}$ MeV, which covers both the stored uncertainty and the store's eight-decimal cut of the CODATA value. The check certifies $r(0.22222204589) < r_{\min}$ and $r(0.22222204830) > r_{\max}$, that neither statement survives one step of $10^{-11}$ inwards (the window is tight at that resolution), the positivity and ordering of the roots there, $p_{1} < 0$ at $0.27 > \tfrac{\pi}{12}$, and strict increase of $r$ on ten sample points of $(0, \tfrac{\pi}{12})$; with the monotonicity above, $\delta_{*}$ lies in the stated window. (Computed in floating point, for orientation only: $\delta_{*} \approx 0.2222220471$; the Koide prediction of the tau mass at $\delta_{*}$ is $1776.969$ MeV, within the stored $1776.93 \pm 0.09$.)

\emph{(ii)} $\tfrac29 < \tfrac{\pi}{12}$ (the check uses the Machin lower bound on $\pi$), and the certified interval for $r(\tfrac29)$ lies in $(206.7703, 206.7704)$. Its lower end exceeds $r_{\max}$ by more than $400\sigma_{\mu}/m_{e}$, and $\sigma_{\mu}/m_{e}$ bounds the standard deviation of the measured ratio from above (the electron's relative uncertainty is $3 \times 10^{-10}$ against the muon's $2.2 \times 10^{-8}$). By monotonicity $\delta_{*} < \tfrac29$, and the check certifies $\tfrac29 - 0.22222204830 > 1.7 \times 10^{-7}$. (Computed in floating point, not part of the proof: with $\delta = \tfrac29$ held fixed and $\lambda$ solved from $r_{\mathrm{obs}}$, $\lambda^{2} = 1.99999915$, $Q - \tfrac23 = -1.4 \times 10^{-7}$ and the predicted tau mass is $1776.967$ MeV, inside the tau window. So $\tfrac29$ alone is not excluded by the data; the joint exactness of $Q = \tfrac23$ and $\delta = \tfrac29$ is. The value $\tfrac29$ for this phase is Brannen's observation, 2006, cited from memory.)

\emph{(iii)} The check finds, by direct search over denominators with integer arithmetic, the least $d$ for which some $k/d$ lies in $[0.22222204589, 0.22222204830]$: $d = 630131$, with $k/d = \tfrac{140029}{630131}$.

\emph{(iv)} $\pi$ is bracketed by Machin's formula $\pi = 16\arctan\tfrac15 - 4\arctan\tfrac{1}{239}$, each arctangent summed to $40$ terms with the first omitted term as error (alternating, decreasing), giving an interval of width below $10^{-50}$ inside $(3.14159265358979, 3.14159265358980)$. The least denominator of a rational in $[\delta_{\mathrm{lo}}/\pi_{\mathrm{hi}}, \delta_{\mathrm{hi}}/\pi_{\mathrm{lo}}]$ is $25249$ (first fraction $\tfrac{1786}{25249}$). If some orbit point $\pm\delta_{*} + \tfrac{j\pi}{6}$ equalled $\tfrac{a}{b}\pi$, then $\delta_{*}/\pi = \pm(\tfrac{a}{b} - \tfrac{j}{6})$ would be a rational of denominator dividing $6b$, so $6b \ge 25249$, $b \ge 4209$. Hence no point of the orbit, and so no channel phase $\chi$ on either slice under any relabelling, is a rational multiple of $\pi$ of denominator at most $4208$.

\emph{Reading of (iv) (argued).} A phase fixed by invariance under a symmetry of finite order $n$ is fixed by a root-of-unity condition and lies in $\tfrac{2\pi}{n}\mathbb{Z}$, possibly after the shifts of the orbit. The stabilisers met in face space are of order at most $6$: the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ left by the real structure (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.real-structure-breaks-source-stabiliser-to-z2}(ii)), the $S_{3}$, the quarter turn $\exp(\tfrac{I_4\pi}{2}P_{d})$ (numbers and the module's complex structure are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, the module read on the tower's floors, where $I_4$ commutes with the tower vectors) and the $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$ of phases with unit product that fixes the cubic family word (ibid.\ (iv)). None of them, nor any finite symmetry of order up to $4208$, can fix the phase that the measured split requires at exact Koide. This is consistent with, and independent of, the stored results that the real-structure completions do not see the channel phase at all and that the cubic word forces nothing.

\emph{(v)} With $\epsilon = 10^{-6}$ the certified difference quotient $(r(\delta(1 + \epsilon)) - r(\delta))/(r(\delta)\epsilon)$ lies in $(12.4, 12.5)$ at both ends of the window. (Floating point: $d\ln r/d\ln\delta = 12.48$ at $\delta_{*}$.) The relabelling signature of Proposition \claimref{families.classification-displaced-gaussian-class-solved-level} is unit sensitivity of the split to a free parameter; the channel phase does not carry it, so a rule fixing the phase would not be flagged by that condition, but it must fix the phase to a relative precision about $12.5$ times finer than the precision wanted for the split ($2.4 \times 10^{-9}$ absolute for the measured precision of $m_{\mu}/m_{e}$).

\emph{Scope.} The result assumes the projection reading of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.coherent-face-vector-real-slices} (the projected coherent vector read as the $\sqrt{m}$ vector) and exact Koide; it says nothing about states whose mass form is not of that form, and nothing about a rule that produces the Koide relation only approximately. It is transport-absent: data, the stored parametrisation and elementary number theory.

synthesis.koide-channel-phase-target-dep.technical: In the $\sqrt{m}$ (circulant) reading, the stored phase target and its no-symmetry-angle bounds use pole masses. With the standard one-loop QED relation between pole and $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ masses, the only non-universal part at first order is $-\kappa\ln m_{i}$, $\kappa = 3\alpha/(2\pi)$, so ratios at a common scale are $\bar{r} = r(1 + \kappa\ln r)$ for every $\mu$. For $\alpha$ between $1/138$ and the stored $\alpha(M_{Z})$ this gives $m_{\mu}/m_{e} \in (210.58, 210.89)$ and, at exact Koide, $\bar{\delta} \in (0.22254, 0.22258)$, more than $3.1 \times 10^{-4}$ above $\delta_{*}$; $\tfrac29$ sits between them, $1800$ times closer to $\delta_{*}$ than the shift. Koide's $Q$ at those masses is off $\tfrac23$ by $(1.0, 1.3) \times 10^{-3}$, a hundred times its pole precision. In the common-scale band the least denominators are $319$ and $367$ (for $\delta/\pi$), so the symmetry-angle bound falls from $4208$ to $61$. Higher orders move the common-scale target by about $10^{-5}$. Under the mass-squared reading only the ratio shift and the Koide defect carry over. Everything is certified interval arithmetic: logarithms by the $\operatorname{atanh}$ series with its geometric remainder, $\pi$ by Machin's formula, sines and cosines by alternating Taylor polynomials.
synthesis.koide-channel-phase-target-dep.lay: The previous result pinned an angle, which encodes the muon-to-electron mass ratio in one reading of this framework (where a vector built from the vacuum is read as the square roots of the masses), to nine decimal places and showed it is not a simple fraction or a simple symmetry angle. But particle masses can be defined in more than one way: the physical mass of a free particle, or a mass that depends on the energy scale at which it is measured. The tiny electromagnetic corrections that relate these definitions shift the mass ratio by about two percent and the angle by about three parts in ten thousand, thousands of times more than the difference between the angle and the often-quoted value $2/9$. So the nine-decimal target, and the conclusion that no symmetry of order up to $4208$ supplies it, hold only if the framework's masses are the physical masses, which is the working choice for now. If the vacuum rule sets masses at a high energy scale, the target moves, it is known far less precisely, and the famous Koide formula itself fails there by about a tenth of a percent.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} As in Proposition \claimref{synthesis.koide-channel-phase-is-no-symmetry-angle}, the projected coherent face vector of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.coherent-face-vector-real-slices} is read as the $\sqrt{m}$ vector; at the Koide depth $\lambda^{2} = 2$ (the null condition of the equal-coefficient member of Proposition \claimref{families.koide-nullity-condition-one-member-invariant}) it is $p_{k} = 1 + \sqrt2\cos(\delta + \tfrac{2\pi k}{3})$ up to a common factor, and $r(\delta) = (p_{2}/p_{1})^{2}$ increases strictly from $1$ to $\infty$ on $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{12})$ (proved there). The imported input is the one-loop QED relation between the pole mass and the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass of a lepton of unit charge, $m^{\mathrm{pole}} = \bar{m}(\mu)\bigl(1 + a(1 + \tfrac32\ln(\mu/\bar{m}))\bigr)$, $a = \alpha/\pi$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-one-loop-qed-pole-mass-relation}; the form used by \cite{Sumino2009}, eq. (6) of \cite{Sumino2009b}). Nothing else is imported; the numbers are the stored pole masses and the stored $\alpha^{-1}(M_{Z}) = 127.951$.

\emph{(i)} For two leptons at a common $\mu$, write $A = 1 + \tfrac32(\ln\mu - \ln m_{j})$, $B = 1 + \tfrac32(\ln\mu - \ln m_{i})$. Then $\bar{m}_{i}/\bar{m}_{j} = (m_{i}/m_{j})(1 + aA)/(1 + aB) = (m_{i}/m_{j})\bigl(1 + a(A - B) + O(a^{2})\bigr)$ and $A - B = \tfrac32\ln(m_{i}/m_{j})$: the $\mu$-dependence and the constant cancel, and with $\kappa = \tfrac32 a = 3\alpha/(2\pi)$, $\bar{r} = r(1 + \kappa\ln r)$ to first order. Equivalently $\bar{m}_{i} \propto m_{i}(1 + \kappa\ln m_{i})$ with a common factor that no ratio and no value of $Q$ sees. At $\mu = \bar{m}_{i}$ for each lepton the logarithm vanishes and every factor is $1 + a$, so ratios of own-scale masses are pole ratios at this order. (The difference between $\bar{m}$ and $m$ inside the logarithm is second order.) The check confirms the coefficient algebra on three rational instances of the logarithms and that the second-order coefficient does not vanish, so the statement is first-order only.

\emph{(ii)} $\bar{r}$ increases with $r$ and with $\kappa$ (as $\ln r > 0$), so over the stored window $r \in (r_{\min}, r_{\max})$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.koide-channel-phase-is-no-symmetry-angle} and $\alpha \in [\tfrac{1}{138}, \alpha(M_{Z})]$ its extremes are at the corners. The check computes them with $\ln$ by $\ln x = k\ln 2 + 2\operatorname{atanh}\tfrac{y - 1}{y + 1}$, $x = 2^{k}y$, $y \in [\tfrac23, \tfrac43]$, the series summed to $40$ terms with the geometric remainder $|z|^{81}/(81(1 - z^{2}))$, $\ln 2 = 2\operatorname{atanh}\tfrac13$, and $\pi$ by Machin's formula; it certifies $\bar{r} \in (210.58, 210.89)$. With $r(\delta)$ evaluated as in the stored check (alternating Taylor polynomials for $\sin$, $\cos$; $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ by integer square roots; outward rounding), $r(0.22254) < \bar{r}_{\min}$ and $r(0.22258) > \bar{r}_{\max}$, and neither survives one step of $10^{-5}$ inwards; $0.22258 < \tfrac{\pi}{12}$. By monotonicity of $r$, $\bar{\delta} \in (0.22254, 0.22258)$ for every admissible $\alpha$ and every $r$ in the window. (Computed in floating point, for orientation: at $\alpha = 1/137.036$, cited from memory, the first-order $\bar{r} = 210.609$ and $\bar{\delta} = 0.222549$; the leading-logarithm resummed form $r^{1 + \kappa}$ gives $210.645$ and $0.222552$. At the stored $\alpha(M_{Z})$ the first-order value is $210.882$ and the resummed one $210.923$. The bracket $[\tfrac{1}{138}, \alpha(M_{Z})]$ is a bracketing choice covering the coupling at the lepton masses and at $M_{Z}$, not a statement about the scheme of $\alpha$ in a fixed-order relation.)

\emph{(iii)} The check recertifies the stored window $\delta_{*} \in (0.22222204589, 0.22222204830)$ against the stored masses, then $0.22254 - 0.22222204830 > 3.1 \times 10^{-4}$ and $> 1800(\tfrac29 - 0.22222204830)$, and $0.22222204830 < \tfrac29 < 0.22254$.

\emph{(iv)} $Q = \sum m_{i}/(\sum\sqrt{m_{i}})^{2}$ is homogeneous of degree zero, so the common factor of (i) drops out and $\bar{Q} = Q(m_{e}, m_{\mu}(1 + \kappa\ln\tfrac{m_{\mu}}{m_{e}}), m_{\tau}(1 + \kappa\ln\tfrac{m_{\tau}}{m_{e}}))$. At the pole masses the check certifies $|Q - \tfrac23| < 10^{-5}$ at the stored centres of $m_{e}$, $m_{\mu}$ and at $m_{\tau} - 0.09$, $m_{\tau}$, $m_{\tau} + 0.09$ MeV; $Q$ increases with $m_{\tau}$ there, since $\partial Q/\partial m_{\tau}$ has the sign of $S_{2} - S_{1}/\sqrt{m_{\tau}}$ with $S_{1} = \sum m_{i}$, $S_{2} = \sum\sqrt{m_{i}}$, and $S_{2} \approx 53.15 > S_{1}/\sqrt{m_{\tau}} \approx 44.65$ (floating point), so the window's ends bound it (this is the stored certified statement, recomputed). At the two ends of the $\kappa$ range, with $m_{\tau}$ in its stored interval, the certified $\bar{Q} - \tfrac23$ lies in $(1.0 \times 10^{-3}, 1.3 \times 10^{-3})$; between the ends $\bar{Q}$ is a smooth function of $\kappa$ with $d\bar{Q}/d\kappa \approx 0.33 > 0$ on the range (floating point), so the bracket holds for every admissible $\alpha$. This is the running-stability observation of \cite{Sumino2009} (there quoted as a correction of about $0.1\%$, $120$ times the experimental error at the time).

\emph{(v)} By direct search over denominators in integer arithmetic, the least $d$ with some $k/d \in [0.22254, 0.22258]$ is $319$ ($\tfrac{71}{319}$), so $\tfrac29$ is outside the band, as (iii) also shows; for $[0.22254/\pi_{\mathrm{hi}}, 0.22258/\pi_{\mathrm{lo}}]$ it is $367$ ($\tfrac{26}{367}$). An orbit point $\pm\bar{\delta} + \tfrac{j\pi}{6} = \tfrac{a}{b}\pi$ would make $\bar{\delta}/\pi$ a rational of denominator dividing $6b$, so $6b \ge 367$ and $b \ge 62$. The band of (ii) is the spread of first-order common-scale targets over the admissible $\alpha$, not a measurement window; the bound says how much the look-elsewhere freedom grows once the mass definition is left open, not that a symmetry angle of order $62$ fits.

\emph{Consequence.} The proved statements of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.koide-channel-phase-is-no-symmetry-angle} stand as statements about pole masses. What changes is their reach: a rule that fixes the face mass form at the frozen point fixes it at a scale far above the lepton thresholds, where (i)-(ii) put its target at $\bar{\delta}$ in the first-order band, more than $10^{5}$ pole-window widths from $\delta_{*}$, and higher orders move it by about $10^{-5}$ (computed in floating point: the running masses at $M_{Z}$ of Xing, Zhang and Zhou, 2008, cited from memory, $0.48657$, $102.718$, $1746.24$ MeV, give $m_{\mu}/m_{e} = 211.11$ and $\delta = 0.22259$, just outside the first-order band). This does not touch (iii) or (v). And by (iv) exact Koide at a common scale contradicts exact Koide at the pole masses at first order, so either the series' masses are pole masses by premise, or a mechanism must cancel the $\kappa\ln m_{i}$ term (the family-gauge cancellation of \cite{Sumino2009} is one such), or the measured pole-mass Koide is not what the face mass form predicts. Under the mass-squared reading, which the store takes as primary and in which the channel phase does not enter the spectrum of source-built completions, (ii), (iii) and (v) have no counterpart; (i) and (iv) carry over unchanged, as statements about the mass ratios and Koide's quotient. The dictionary in force is pole masses, provisionally; under it the stored statements stand. The result is transport-absent: QED at one loop, the stored masses and the stored parametrisation.
